assumptions: The derivation is not strictly necessary or is broader than users reasonably expect.
uncertainty_note: Necessity cannot be fully determined from the brief description alone; the threat is grounded in the explicit enrichment/profiling activity.

title: Data subjects may be unaware that historical location data is analyzed for routine inference
description: Using stored location history across sessions to infer daily routine and movement patterns may not be apparent to data subjects, especially when they expect storage or basic service use rather than behavioral profiling.
assumptions: Users were not clearly informed about this specific analytics purpose.

title: Data subjects may lack control over profiling from location history
description: The analytics service may process historical location data for routine and movement-pattern derivation without giving data subjects meaningful preference, consent, or opt-out controls for this specific profiling activity.
assumptions: No granular controls exist for analytics use of stored location history.
uncertainty_note: The presence or absence of user controls is not specified; this is a plausible risk tied to the described profiling use.

title: Cross-session location-history analytics may violate data minimization
description: Querying and processing historical location data across sessions to derive routines and movement patterns may involve more personal data, and more detailed data, than is necessary for the analytics purpose.
assumptions: Equivalent functionality could be achieved with less detailed or less extensive data.

title: Profiling based on location history may lack an appropriate lawful basis or safeguards
description: Deriving daily routine and movement patterns from location history is a potentially intrusive profiling activity that may create lawfulness concerns if not properly justified, limited, and safeguarded.
assumptions: The system operates in a regime where such profiling requires a clear lawful basis and proportionality assessment.
uncertainty_note: Actual noncompliance depends on the applicable legal basis, notices, and safeguards, which are not provided.

title: Inferred insights enable linkage of multiple health events to the same individual profile
description: The Health Analytics Service returns derived health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags that can act as a stable behavioral/health profile. By sharing these inferences to the app, the source enables records across time or contexts to be linked back to the same individual.

title: App can link inferred insights over time into a persistent user profile
description: On receipt, the Companion Mobile App can aggregate successive inferred insights, trend flags, and summaries into a longitudinal profile, increasing the ability to link separate observations and sessions to the same user.

title: Inferred health insights are identifying through revealing attributes
description: The data flow contains revealing attributes such as health-condition risk indicators and behavioral routine summaries. Even without an explicit name, these attributes may allow the data subject to be identified or singled out, especially when combined with app/account context.

title: Returned inferences can become attributable evidence about the user
description: The analytics output constitutes a data record asserting health-related risks, routines, or trends about a specific user. Once shared, these records may later be used as evidence that the user had certain conditions, behaviors, or risk patterns, reducing deniability.

title: Transmission metadata may create attributable evidence
description: Metadata associated with the transmission of inferred insights, such as timing, sender/recipient context, or session linkage, can help attribute the returned health insights to a particular user and interaction.

title: Displayed analytics responses may reveal existence of sensitive health inferences
description: When the app receives and presents risk indicators or trend flags, the system response itself can reveal that the user is associated with a particular health concern or monitored routine, enabling detection of an item of interest.

title: Analytics may disclose highly sensitive inferred health data beyond what the app strictly needs
description: Health-condition risk indicators and trend flags are highly sensitive inferred data. Returning them from the analytics service to the app may disclose more sensitive data types than are strictly necessary for the app's immediate functionality.
uncertainty_note: Applies if the app could fulfill its purpose with less sensitive or less explicit insight outputs; the exact necessity is not fully specified.

title: Returned insights may be more granular than necessary
description: Routine summaries and trend flags may include fine-grained behavioral or health detail. If the app only needs coarse guidance, sending detailed inferred indicators creates unnecessary disclosure of granularity.
uncertainty_note: Granularity needs are not specified, so this depends on the app's functional requirements.

title: Propagation of inferred health insights into the mobile app increases exposure
description: By receiving the analytics output, the app becomes another processing location for sensitive inferred health data. This propagation increases exposure and may be unnecessary if insights could remain server-side or be presented in a less disclosive form.
uncertainty_note: Depends on whether local app access to the full inferred insights is functionally required.

title: User may be unaware that sensitive health inferences are being returned to the app
description: The flow involves derived health-condition risk indicators and trend analyses, which may not be obvious to the data subject. If the analytics service shares these inferences back to the app without clear notice, the user may be unaware of this processing and disclosure.

title: App may not provide control over receipt and use of inferred insights
description: Once the app receives inferred health insights, the data subject may lack meaningful preferences or consent controls over whether such sensitive inferences are shown, stored, or further used within the app.
uncertainty_note: The existence of user controls is not described; threat applies if such controls are absent or insufficient.

title: Sharing inferred health insights may violate data minimization
description: Returning health-condition risk indicators, routine summaries, and trend flags to the app may involve processing and disclosure of more personal data than necessary for the stated functionality, especially given the sensitivity of inferred health data.
uncertainty_note: Depends on whether each inferred field is strictly necessary for the app's purpose.

title: Insufficient data subject controls over inferred health data in the app
description: If the app does not support adequate access, preference, rectification, or deletion controls for received inferred health insights, the destination processing may create GDPR-style noncompliance risks around data subject rights.
uncertainty_note: Control mechanisms are not described, so this is contingent on their absence.

title: Processing inferred sensitive health data may raise lawfulness concerns
description: The analytics service shares inferred health-condition risk indicators with the app, which may constitute sensitive health-related personal data or similarly sensitive inferences. If the lawful basis, safeguards, or constraints on such inference processing are inadequate, this flow creates regulatory noncompliance risk.
uncertainty_note: This depends on jurisdiction and whether inferred risk indicators are treated as sensitive health data in the applicable regime.

title: App-generated risk indicators enable linkage of multiple observations about the same user
description: By displaying trends and inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals, the app shares a profile-like summary that can link multiple measurements, behaviors, and time periods to the same wearer. The source process creates and discloses a coherent longitudinal view that increases linkability of the user's health-related data.

title: Dashboard content contains revealing health attributes that can identify the wearer in context
description: The data flow carries highly revealing attributes, namely inferred condition indicators and trends related to eating-disorder or diabetes risk. Even if no explicit name is included, such sensitive health attributes can make the wearer identifiable in context, especially on a personal mobile device or observable session.

title: Displayed inferred condition indicators can become attributable evidence about the user
description: The source process presents health-risk inferences to the user in a form that may later serve as evidence that the user was associated with particular symptoms, trends, or risk states. Screens, logs, or retained app state could make those claims attributable and harder for the user to deny.

title: Presence of risk indicators in the app response reveals existence of sensitive health inferences
description: The system response itself reveals that the system has inferred eating-disorder or diabetes-related risk signals for the wearer. Anyone able to observe the dashboard output or notification-like display can detect the existence of a sensitive condition-related item of interest.

title: Displaying inferred condition indicators may disclose highly sensitive health data beyond what is necessary
description: The app dashboard shares inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals with the user. Such inferred health-condition indicators are highly sensitive personal data; if the dashboard's functional goal could be met with less sensitive or less explicit feedback, this source-side disclosure would exceed necessity.
uncertainty_note: The necessity of showing explicit condition-risk indicators versus more generic wellness feedback is not fully established from the provided context.

title: User may be unaware that the app derives and displays condition-risk inferences
description: If the app dashboard presents eating-disorder or diabetes risk signals without clear explanation, the wearer may not be aware that their personal data has been analyzed to derive these sensitive inferences. The source process causes this unawareness by surfacing results without necessarily exposing the underlying processing logic or scope.

title: Displaying inferred sensitive health-risk signals may create lawfulness and automated-processing compliance issues
description: The source process communicates inferred eating-disorder or diabetes risk indicators, which are sensitive health-related personal data. If these inferences are generated or acted upon without an appropriate lawful basis, suitable safeguards, or required transparency around automated profiling, the processing may be non-compliant.
uncertainty_note: Applicable legal obligations depend on jurisdiction and whether the indicators are used for significant decisions or merely informational feedback.

title: Source shares a full health and location dataset that enables strong linkage

This increases the ability to correlate records about the same individual across datasets or processing contexts.

title: Source discloses identifiable health and location data through quasi-identifiers
description: The source sends a full health and location dataset whose combination of attributes can make individuals identifiable even if direct names are absent. Fine-grained location plus health-related attributes are strong quasi-identifiers.

title: Transfer metadata may reveal identified or identifying information
description: The data flow to a third-party cloud provider may expose identifying information in communication or file metadata, such as account identifiers, tenant names, object names, or dataset labels indicating health-related content.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not explicitly mention transport or file metadata contents, so this is a plausible but not certain identifying threat at the flow level.

title: Destination receives revealing attributes sufficient to identify data subjects

title: Shared dataset can become attributable evidence about individuals
description: By transferring full health and location records to the cloud provider, the source creates data records that can later be used as evidence to attribute conditions, movements, or behaviors to specific individuals, reducing deniability.

title: Transfer metadata can create attributable evidence of data subjects or actions

title: Hosted and replicated records may be used to deny individuals plausible deniability
description: Once stored and replicated at the cloud provider, the data may serve as durable evidence about a person's health status or location history, making later denial of associated claims more difficult.

title: Observed transfer to a cloud provider can reveal the existence of sensitive processing
description: Observation of this communication flow can reveal that health analytics data and full health/location datasets are being transferred to a third-party cloud provider, exposing the existence of sensitive processing activities or datasets of interest.

title: Source shares highly sensitive data types with the cloud provider
description: The source discloses full health and location data to the cloud provider. These are highly sensitive personal data types, and sharing them with an external party may exceed what is strictly necessary depending on the hosting need.

title: Source transfers data at finer granularity than may be needed
description: Sending the full health and location dataset suggests disclosure at a very fine-grained level rather than a minimized or aggregated form, increasing privacy exposure to the cloud provider.

title: Source transfers an excessive amount of personal data
description: The flow includes the full health and location dataset in addition to analytics data and models, indicating a large volume of personal data is shared with the external provider.

title: Source propagates personal data to an external party
description: The source makes personal data accessible to a third-party cloud hosting provider for hosting and replication, which is a propagation of sensitive data beyond the analytics service itself.

title: Source exposes personal data to a predetermined external party
description: The source shares sensitive personal data with a known third party, the cloud hosting provider. This increases exposure to an additional party beyond the originating analytics service.

title: Destination may retain replicated data longer than necessary
description: Because the cloud provider hosts and replicates the full dataset, the destination may keep copies, backups, or replicas for longer than functionally necessary, increasing disclosure risk over time.
uncertainty_note: Retention duration is not specified, but replication commonly increases persistence and the number of retained copies.

title: Destination-side hosting exposes data to additional provider-controlled parties
description: At the destination, hosted and replicated storage can make the dataset accessible within the cloud provider's operational environment to additional predetermined parties such as administrators or subprocessors, increasing exposure.

title: Data subjects may be unaware their full health and location data is hosted by a third party

uncertainty_note: No notice or transparency mechanism is described, so unawareness is plausible but not certain.

title: Third-party hosting and replication can hinder erasure or rectification
description: Once the cloud provider stores and replicates the full dataset, data subjects may have reduced practical ability to ensure correction or deletion across all hosted copies and replicas.

title: Sharing the full dataset with a cloud provider may violate data minimization
description: The source transfers the full health and location dataset, along with analytics data and models, to an external provider. If full-detail hosting is not strictly necessary, this creates a GDPR data minimization non-compliance risk.

title: External hosting of sensitive health and location data may lack an appropriate lawful basis
description: Sending sensitive health and location data to a third-party cloud provider may create lawfulness concerns if the transfer, hosting, and replication are not properly justified under the applicable legal basis and safeguards.
uncertainty_note: The lawful basis, processor arrangements, and safeguards are not provided, so this is a compliance risk rather than a confirmed violation.

title: Replication at the destination may conflict with storage limitation
description: Hosting and replication at the cloud provider can increase the number and persistence of copies, creating a risk that personal data is stored longer than necessary.

title: Third-party replication can undermine effective data subject rights handling
description: If the cloud provider stores multiple replicas of the full dataset, fulfilling access, rectification, and erasure requests across all copies may become difficult, creating a risk of insufficient support for data subject rights.
